newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton dines with Yeltsin, upbeat on summit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton dines with Yeltsin, upbeat on summit.

text.p: A wheelchair-bound U.S. President Bill Clinton dined with Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday and came away optimistic about narrowing their differences on NATO expansion in summit talks on Friday.

"I think he (Yeltsin) really came here to do business," Clinton told White House spokesman Mike McCurry after more than two hours at a salmon-and-reindeer dinner hosted by Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari.
McCurry said the summit had got off to a good start.

"The president and Yeltsin were clearly striking a tone for the meeting which seemed to be very positive," he said. "There was a lot of banter back and forth and the president was engaging Yeltsin, telling stories about some of their previous meetings."

Clinton and Yeltsin, who was bouncing back into the global spotlight after being sidelined for more than six months because of heart surgery and pneumonia, arrived in Helsinki within hours of each other for their first meeting in nearly a year.

The U.S. president, hobbled by a knee injury in a freak accident that forced him to have surgery last Friday, was wheeled off his jumbo jet and on to a catering truck that lowered him to the airport tarmac.

Before the two-day summit, which was delayed by one day by Clinton's injury, Russian officials unleashed a torrent of tough talk about NATO expansion to the east. But Yeltsin took a softer line on his arrival, telling reporters compromise was possible.
Clinton responded in kind when asked about Yeltsin's remarks, saying: "I was quite encouraged."
"I felt good about it. I'm looking forward to it."
The important business of the summit was to take place on Friday at Ahtisaari's secluded official residence.
Clinton hoped to persuade Yeltsin NATO plans for enlargement were no threat to Russia and would enhance European security.
An alliance summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to be the first former Soviet bloc nations to start membership talks.
U.S. officials have been adamant that NATO exapansion will go forward despite objections from the Kremlin, which sees the scheme as a threat to its security.
"I don't expect them to change their views and they shouldn't expect us to change our views," National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told reporters.
In addition to the future shape of NATO -- and Russia's relationship with it -- Clinton and Yeltsin were to discuss arms control and Russia's transformation to a market economy.
But U.S. officials sought to play down expectations.
"There's a lot of very difficult work that lies ahead and some differences that will be difficult to bridge," McCurry said.

A key U.S. arms control aim was to win a Russian pledge to ratify soon the START-2 strategic arms reduction treaty, which would reduce U.S. and Russian arsenals of nuclear warheads to 3,500 warheads each, a senior U.S. official said.
Another U.S. official said on the economic front, Clinton would press for significant changes in Russian legal and tax treatment of commercial properties and investments.
The U.S. president was prepared to offer "a package of incentives for U.S. investors to respond to those changes".
The Clinton administration has asked Congress to provide $900 million in aid to Russia and the newly independent states of Eastern Europe this year, up from $614 million last year.
Clinton told reporters his knee injury had not proved an impediment to his work on the summit.
McCurry said Yeltsin was "not as vibrant as I've seen him in the past" at the dinner but was "certainly engaged in the conversation with Clinton...and very focused on things".
"He looks like he's recovering from surgery," he said. "And, you know, Clinton obviously looks like he's recovering from surgery."
